faqs.a: When three things are true: the new rate is clearly lower than your current average, the monthly payment fits your budget, and you will not run up new balances on the freed cards. Miss any one of these and consolidation usually backfires.
faqs.q: When is debt consolidation a good idea?

faqs.a: Temporarily, a little — the new loan triggers a hard inquiry and lowers your average account age. But paying down revolving balances lowers utilization, which often lifts your score within months. For disciplined borrowers the net effect is usually positive.
faqs.q: Does consolidation hurt my credit score?

faqs.a: A 0% balance-transfer card wins if you can clear the debt inside the promo window (usually 12–18 months) — but the rate after the promo is brutal, and transfer fees run 3–5%. A consolidation loan is better for larger balances you need years to repay.
faqs.q: Balance transfer card or consolidation loan?

faqs.a: Because term matters as much as rate. Cutting your rate from 18% to 10% but stretching from 32 to 60 months can still raise total interest. Always compare total interest paid, not just the monthly figure — this calculator shows both.
faqs.q: Why does a lower monthly payment sometimes cost more overall?

faqs.a: Origination fees (1–5% of the loan), balance-transfer fees (3–5%), prepayment penalties on old loans, and annual fees. A 'low rate' with a 4% origination fee can be worse than a slightly higher rate with no fee. Add fees to the loan amount when comparing.
faqs.q: What fees should I watch for?

debt-consolidation-calculator.formula:
Current plan: simulate month by month — interest = balance x APR/12, subtract payment, repeat until zero.
New loan payment M = L x i(1+i)^n / ((1+i)^n - 1).
Monthly saving = current payment - new payment.
Total saving = current total paid - new total paid.

keyFacts: Consolidation replaces several debts with one loan, ideally at a lower rate.
It only saves money if the new APR is lower than your current weighted average.
Stretching the term lowers the monthly payment but can raise total interest — watch both.
Origination fees of 1–5% can quietly eat the savings; include them in the loan amount.
The biggest risk is behavioral: new debt on freed-up cards wipes out every gain.

debt-consolidation-calculator.quickAnswer: On ₹200,000 of debt at 18% APR with ₹8,000 monthly payments, you would pay ₹52,559 in interest over 32 months. A 10% consolidation loan over 36 months cuts the payment to ₹6,453 and total interest to ₹32,324 — saving ₹20,235 overall. Consolidation wins when the new rate is meaningfully lower and you stop adding new debt.
debt-consolidation-calculator.tagline: Compare juggling multiple debts against one consolidation loan — see the real savings.
debt-consolidation-calculator.workedExample:
Debt ₹200,000 at 18% APR, paying ₹8,000/month; consolidation loan at 10% APR over 36 months:
1. Current plan: 32 months, total paid ₹252,558.56, interest ₹52,558.56.
2. New payment: i = 0.10/12 = 0.008333; M = 200,000 x 0.008333 x 1.34818 / 0.34818 = ₹6,453.44.
3. New total = 6,453.44 x 36 = ₹232,323.75; interest = ₹32,323.75.
4. Monthly saving = 8,000 - 6,453.44 = ₹1,546.56; total saving = 252,558.56 - 232,323.75 = ₹20,234.81.
Consolidation wins.
